prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I woke from a bird hitting the window, almost, I thought, hard enough to break it. The sun rose knowingly. I slid the sash up and stuck my head out like someone in an Italian movie. A flicker lay on its back—stunned—but it was blinking steady as a railroad crossing. Was there misery to put out? Would it come to its "senses"? I thought where were you when bark beetles killed half my trees? Then I remembered, sleepily, reading that flickers mostly eat ants. I went back to sleep for half an hour, and dreamed, as I often do, of horses. When next I looked, the bird still lay still, still blinking. Maybe, I thought, it can't roll over. So I went down and rolled it over. Terrified by my touch, it came to life and flop- hopped down the hill into some sagebrush. It didn't fly, but it didn't seem broken, either. I tried to find it later. No luck. Whether it lived and flew off, or died thrust into a bush, was, apparently, none of my business. If it were thrust into a bush, I knew the ants wouldn't wait for the guest of honor to start dinner.

outputs.L2:
A bird striking the window woke me; it sounded, I nearly believed, forceful enough to shatter the glass. The sun was coming up with an air of certainty. I raised the window and leaned my head outside, as if I were acting in an Italian film. A flicker was lying on its back, dazed, though its eyes kept blinking with the regularity of a railroad signal.

Was it suffering in a way that needed ending? Would it recover its awareness? I found myself thinking, Where were you when bark beetles destroyed half of my trees? Then, still half asleep, I recalled having read that flickers mainly feed on ants. I returned to bed for another thirty minutes and dreamed, as I frequently do, about horses.

When I checked again, the bird remained motionless, still blinking. Perhaps, I thought, it simply couldn’t turn itself upright. So I went outside and flipped it over. Frightened by my hand, it suddenly revived and half-flopped, half-hopped down the slope into a patch of sagebrush. It did not take flight, but it did not appear badly injured either. Later I tried to locate it, without success. Whether it survived and eventually flew away, or died wedged inside a bush, seemed, in the end, not to be my concern. And if it had ended up dead in the brush, I knew the ants would not wait for the guest of honor before beginning their meal.
outputs.L3:
A flicker struck the window hard enough to wake the narrator. When they looked outside, they saw the bird lying stunned on the ground beneath the glass. It was on its back, motionless except for the faint sign that it was still alive: it was blinking.

For a moment, the narrator wondered whether the bird was suffering. The question came with a strange tenderness and helplessness, because there was so little to be done and no way to know what the bird was feeling. They thought, too, about what they knew of flickers—that they are birds that mostly eat ants, probing the ground for them with their long tongues. That small fact made the bird seem both ordinary and particular: a wild creature with its own habits, suddenly interrupted.

The narrator went back to bed and eventually fell asleep again. In sleep, they dreamed of horses. But when they woke and checked the window once more, the flicker was still there, still lying on its back where it had fallen.

This time, the narrator went outside. They approached the bird and gently rolled it over. The flicker did not immediately fly away, but it was no longer entirely helpless. Slowly, it revived enough to move, managing an awkward flop-hop toward the sagebrush. The narrator watched as it disappeared into the cover of the brush, not restored exactly, but no longer stranded on its back beneath the window.

Later, the narrator looked for the flicker again and could not find it. There was no sign to tell whether it had recovered, died, or been taken by another animal. In the end, the narrator had to accept that the bird’s fate could not be known. It belonged to the wildness beyond the window, beyond certainty, and beyond the narrator’s control.
outputs.L4:
A sharp, sudden thud struck the window, so loud and close that for a moment I thought something inside the room had broken. When I looked up, the glass was still intact, faintly trembling in its frame, but outside, on the ground beneath it, lay a flicker.

The bird was on its back, wings partly spread, feet drawn up stiffly toward its breast. Its spotted feathers and barred wings, which must have looked so swift and precise in flight, now seemed awkward and exposed against the pale dust. For several moments I only stood at the window and watched. I did not know whether it was dead, dying, or merely stunned. Its body had the stillness of something finished, yet there was also something unfinished about it, as though life had not quite left but had withdrawn to some hidden center.

I went outside cautiously. The day was quiet, and the bird lay in the narrow strip of ground near the house, where the sagebrush began. I knelt beside it but did not touch it at first. Its eyes were open. That was the most troubling part: not blank, exactly, but not aware in any human way I could understand. The eyes seemed to receive the world without answering it. I watched for breathing and thought I saw the faintest movement in the breast, then doubted myself. The flicker’s long beak pointed upward at an unnatural angle. One wing was folded beneath it; the other was loosened, showing a flash of yellow underneath.

I wondered what I ought to do. If the bird was dying, perhaps it was better to leave it alone. If it was only stunned, perhaps handling it would frighten it or do further harm. The window, which to me was a boundary between indoors and outdoors, had been invisible to the bird. It had flown into a piece of reflected sky and fallen. Now I stood over it with the uneasy feeling that I was both responsible and not responsible. I had not struck it down, yet my house had. I had not meant to deceive it, yet the glass had offered a false opening in the air.

The flicker did not move. Ants had not found it yet. No cat or hawk circled nearby. The world seemed to be waiting, though of course the world was not waiting at all. It was only I who felt suspended, trying to decide whether compassion required action or restraint.

At last I took a small stick and gently touched the bird’s foot. The claws closed weakly, then opened again. That small response changed everything. It was alive. Still, I hesitated. I did not know how fragile its bones were or whether its neck or wing was broken. I had the absurd thought that perhaps it would right itself when it was ready, as if dignity required that I give it time. But the longer it lay there on its back, the more helpless it seemed, and the more impossible it became simply to watch.

I set the stick aside and reached down with my hand. The bird was lighter than I expected, all feathers and heat and delicate structure. Carefully, as if turning a page that might tear, I rolled it over onto its feet. For a second it collapsed forward, its beak touching the ground. Then it gathered itself. The movement was not graceful. It was a shudder, a confused reassembly of balance. One wing dragged slightly; then it pulled the wing closer. Its head tilted. The eye, bright now with alarm, seemed suddenly to recognize the world as dangerous.

I stepped back.

The flicker remained still for another moment, crouched low in the dust. Then, with a burst of awkward energy, it hopped toward the sagebrush. It did not fly. It half-ran, half-fluttered, vanishing beneath the gray-green branches. The brush trembled once, then became still. I could no longer see the bird, though I knew it was there, hidden in the shade and stems, recovering or failing where I could not follow.

I stood outside for a while, looking at the place where it had disappeared. I wanted a clear ending: for the flicker to rise suddenly into the air, restored, beating its yellow-lined wings toward the open land. Or else, if it had to die, I wanted to know that too. But nature rarely offers such conclusions to those who merely pass through as witnesses. The bird had moved beyond my sight, and with that it had moved beyond my knowledge.

All I had done was turn it over. Perhaps that was enough. Perhaps it was not. It might have recovered fully and flown away later, leaving no sign of its collision except a faint mark on the window. It might have died under the sagebrush before evening. Some predator might have found it. The possibilities remained, each one equally hidden.

I went back inside, but the sound of the impact stayed with me. So did the sight of the bird lying upside down, alive but unable to help itself. I thought about how often human responsibility begins in uncertainty, not in power: we see something hurt, we do not understand it completely, and still we must decide whether to act. Yet even when we act, our part is small. We can roll the bird over. We can give it a chance. We cannot command its recovery, follow it into the brush, or know the final shape of its fate.

Outside, the window reflected the sky again. To me it was a window. To a bird, it might still be air.
outputs.L5:
**The Italian Was**

The Italian was a quiet traveler with a worn leather notebook and a smile that seemed to carry stories from every city he had visited. He spoke softly, choosing his words with care, as if each sentence were a small piece of music. Wherever he went, people noticed his warmth, his love for food, and the way he described his homeland with pride.

He spoke of narrow streets in Rome, bright mornings in Florence, and evenings in Venice when the water reflected the golden light of the setting sun. To him, Italy was not only a place on a map; it was a collection of memories, flavors, voices, and traditions.

The Italian was especially passionate about cooking. He believed that a simple meal could bring people together better than any speech. A plate of pasta, fresh bread, olive oil, and a shared conversation were, to him, signs of a good life.

In every town he visited, he left behind kindness and took with him a new story. The Italian was more than a traveler; he was a reminder that culture lives through people, through their memories, and through the way they share them with the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short literary flash fiction piece in first person about waking up to a bird hitting a window, with dry humor, nature imagery, and an ambiguous ending.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn, a bird struck my bedroom window with the sound of a fist knocking politely on the wrong century.

I woke upright, heart conducting a small, incompetent orchestra. Outside, the glass held a perfect gray smudge, feathered at the edges like bad watercolor. Below it, on the sill, a sparrow sat in the gutter of morning light, blinking as if it had just remembered an appointment elsewhere.

The world around it was offensively beautiful. The maples shook dew from their leaves. The sky blushed peach over the roofs. Somewhere, a squirrel made a managerial decision in the lilacs. Spring had arrived with its usual tactlessness, all fragrance and reproduction, while I stood in my pajamas holding a mug that said *World’s Best Dad*, despite having no children and no measurable authority over worlds.

The sparrow tipped its head. I tipped mine back.

“Same,” I said.

It opened its beak, but no sound came. Perhaps it was stunned. Perhaps it had seen, in the reflective glass, a blue corridor through the house, a continuation of sky, and believed it. I couldn’t blame it. I had made worse choices with less convincing evidence.

I considered going outside, scooping it into a shoebox, Googling what to do. Instead I watched. This is what separates humans from animals: the capacity to delay kindness in favor of research.

The bird fluffed itself once, violently, becoming for a moment all feather and indignation. Then it hopped to the edge of the sill and looked through the window at me—past me, maybe—into the dim room where the unmade bed crouched like an accusation.

Behind me, something moved.

I turned. Nothing, of course. Only the closet door ajar, the mirror catching a strip of pale sky, my own face floating in it with the expression of someone expecting a verdict.

When I looked back, the sill was empty.

There was no bird in the grass, no broken wing, no small body surrendered to the bright, efficient ants. Just the fading mark on the window, already loosening in the sun, and beyond it the maples lifting their green hands as if they had seen nothing, which was very much their style.

Then came another knock—soft, deliberate—from the glass.

This time, I was already awake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Lydia Davis–style micro-essay about finding a stunned flicker outside a house, including thoughts about ants, bark beetles, and whether helping the bird matters.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Lydia Davis’s exact style, but here is an original spare micro-essay with a similarly brief, observant, unsettled quality:

**The Flicker**

Outside the house, near the hose, there was a flicker lying on its side.

At first I thought it was dead because it allowed me to think so. Then it moved its eye.

The eye seemed not frightened, only occupied.

I put on gloves. This seemed both practical and theatrical. I lifted the bird and set it in a box with a towel. Its spotted breast rose and fell. Its feet, made for clinging to bark, curled around nothing.

Earlier that week I had noticed ants entering a crack by the steps. I had thought: They have found something, or they are making something. I had not helped or stopped them. I had only watched, with the feeling that watching was a kind of decision.

The trees beyond the yard had bark beetles. You could see the fine dust at the base of the trunks. The beetles were small and purposeful and, taken together, fatal. No one bird could matter to them. No one tree could persuade them.

The flicker sat in the box for an hour. Then another. I kept looking in, as if my looking might help it gather itself.

It is difficult to know what counts. To the ants, the bird would have been an event. To the beetles, nothing. To me, for that afternoon, it was the center of the yard, and the yard was the center of what could be done.

When I opened the box, the flicker did not leave at once.

Then it did.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a concise personal narrative set in the rural American West where the narrator discovers an injured bird, tries minimally to help it, and reflects wryly on death and indifference.
counterfactuals.output:
Out past the last cattle guard, where the county road gives up and turns to powder, I found the bird in the ditch.

It was a meadowlark, I think, though I’ve been wrong about birds before and they’ve never corrected me. One wing lay open in the dust like a bad hand of cards. The morning was already hot. Grasshoppers ticked through the cheatgrass, and somewhere beyond the fence a windmill complained in its long, reasonable way.

I stood over it awhile with my coffee going cold in my hand. The bird looked at me with one black bead of an eye, not pleading exactly. More like it had noticed I was there and was waiting to see what kind of nuisance I intended to be.

I got a shoebox from the truck, the one that used to hold fuel filters, and set it in the shade of a sagebrush. I poured a little water into the lid of my thermos and nudged it close. The bird did not thank me. It did not drink. It breathed fast, as if keeping up with something already leaving.

That was the extent of my heroism.

I thought about driving it the forty miles to town, where someone at the feed store might know a woman who knew a woman who took in broken things. But the truck was low on gas, and I had fence to mend, and there is a point at which mercy starts looking a lot like errands.

So I left it there, boxed in shade, with water it didn’t want.

By evening the wind had come up and blown dust over everything, smoothing the road, the tracks, my intentions. When I stopped on the way back, the box was tipped over and empty. Maybe the bird had found some last pocket of strength and flung itself into the grass. Maybe a fox had found it. Maybe death, for once, was efficient.

The West is good at that kind of shrug. Sky overhead, bones underneath, work in between. I drove home with the windows down, feeling neither cruel nor kind, which may be the most honest a person gets.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a brief, observational prose piece about a window strike by a bird, blending dreamlike details, dark comedy, and philosophical resignation.
counterfactuals.output:
The sound was not a thud so much as a decision.

I looked up from my coffee and found the window holding, for one vanishing second, the pale imprint of a bird: wings flung wide, head turned slightly, as if it had just remembered an appointment elsewhere. Then the mark faded, and below it, in the lavender weeds by the drainpipe, the bird lay on its back with its feet arranged like punctuation.

The morning went on being absurdly beautiful. Clouds dragged their white furniture across the sky. A fly inspected the glass at the exact site of impact, perhaps hoping for instructions. Inside, the toaster released two slices with the solemnity of a crematorium.

I went outside in slippers. The bird was small, anonymous, gray-brown—the kind of creature that spends its whole life avoiding biography. One bead-black eye reflected me upside down, which seemed fair. I had also been moving quickly toward invisible things.

For a moment I expected it to revive, to spring up embarrassed, shake off death like a bad hat, and explain that it had mistaken the reflected maple for the world. But the maple was the world too, in its way, and so was the glass, and so was the mistake.

I fetched a garden trowel. The bird weighed almost nothing, less than an apology. I buried it beneath the hydrangea, where last year’s petals still clung like old receipts. When I came back in, the window was clean again, showing trees, sky, and my own face hovering faintly over everything, complicit and breakable.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a first-person vignette in a sparse, literary voice: a bird hits the window at dawn, the narrator rolls it over, it disappears into sagebrush, and the ending mentions ants.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn a bird struck the window with a sound like a small fist.

I found it below the glass, on its side in the pale dirt, one wing folded under. Its eye was open. The sky had not yet decided on blue.

I went out in my bare feet and knelt. The ground was cold. I turned the bird over with two fingers. It weighed almost nothing, a little pulse of feathers and fear.

For a moment it lay still. Then it gathered itself, not flying, but vanishing by degrees into the sagebrush, a brown flicker among brown stems.

I stood there until the light came on the hills.

Later, when I looked again, there was only the mark in the dust, and ants.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
